title: Why I finally moved off REST for internal tools
body:
Spent a weekend rewriting our internal admin API in tRPC. The old REST version had drifted for two years - routes that didn't match the client's expectations anymore, a Postman collection nobody trusted, and a types package we had to remember to rebuild by hand.

The biggest win was immediate: end-to-end types. No more guessing whether GET /admin/users/:id returns lastLoginAt as a string or a number.

What got worse: caching. REST gave us free HTTP caching semantics we didn't realize we were leaning on. We had to rebuild some of that manually on the client.

The migration trap: our auth middleware assumed a REST-style request object, and tRPC's context setup runs before that middleware in a way I didn't expect - cost me an entire afternoon to untangle.

title: Async/await gotchas that still trip me up in Node
body:
Every few weeks I still forget that `forEach` does not await async work and that a rejected promise without a catch can vanish inside a fire-and-forget loop.

My current checklist is small but reliable: promise boundaries, unhandled rejection listeners, re-entrancy, and aborting long-running tasks when the request goes away.

```js
await Promise.all(tasks.map(task => runTask(task)));
// treat each task as a boundary, not as a side effect
```

The bug pattern I keep revisiting is not about the async syntax itself - it's the assumptions around when the work is actually complete.

title: Show stackTrace: a tiny CLI for scaffolding Express routes
body:
I built a tiny CLI to stop copy-pasting the same route/controller boilerplate on every Express project. It turns a resource name into a ready-to-edit folder structure with handlers and tests.

The thing I wanted most was less ceremony and more confidence. The generator is intentionally opinionated, so we can keep style consistent without turning the project into a framework.

```sh
stacktrace scaffold users
# generates routes, controller, service, tests
```

It isn't meant to replace architecture choices; it's just there to remove the repetitive parts so the team can focus on the risky bits.

title: Debugging a slow memory leak in a long-running Express server
body:
We had a node process that looked healthy in logs but kept consuming memory until the machine started swapping. The first clue was a steady climb in event listeners, even when the app looked idle.

The fix was simple but annoying: tracing where the listeners were bound and ensuring the unsubscribe path ran on shutdown and on retry.

```sh
node --inspect-brk app.js
# pause, take heap snapshot, compare listener counts
```

The memory leak wasn't caused by the framework; it was a subtle lifecycle bug in a shared queue that never removed listeners when the consumer was replaced.

title: Tailwind is great until your class names become a paragraph
body:
I like Tailwind. I really do. But I hit a point yesterday where I had to horizontally scroll through a component just to understand its styling.

The component had a grid, responsive padding, dark mode, hover state, disabled state and two slightly different breakpoints. The markup looked like a ransom note.

I ended up extracting the repeated pieces into a small component instead of reaching for `@apply` everywhere. Much easier to read now.

I don't think long Tailwind class lists automatically mean bad code. But when the HTML becomes harder to understand than the CSS it replaced, that's probably a sign to split something up.

title: The React useEffect cleanup I forgot about
PostgreSQL indexes: I finally stopped adding them blindly
body:
I used to treat indexes like free performance upgrades. Query is slow? Add an index. Problem solved, right?

Not quite.

I had a table where we kept adding indexes because different queries were slow. Eventually writes got noticeably more expensive and some of the indexes weren't being used at all.

Running `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` before changing anything made a huge difference. Sometimes the problem was the query, sometimes the data distribution, and sometimes the index I thought would help simply wasn't useful for that particular query.

Indexes are great. They're also not free. I wish I had learned that before creating eight of them on one table.

title: TypeScript made this bug impossible to ship
body:
Had an API response where `status` used to be a string but was changed to an object on the backend.

The frontend had several places doing stuff like `if (status === "active")`, so without types we'd probably have shipped a UI that silently stopped showing active accounts.

Because the response type was shared, TypeScript started complaining in six different places immediately.

I know people joke about TypeScript being annoying when you're moving quickly, but this is exactly the kind of annoying I want. It complained before the bug became somebody else's ticket.

title: SQLite is underrated for small Node projects
body:
Started a side project with PostgreSQL because that's what I normally use. Then I realized I was the only person running it, the database had about twelve tables, and the entire thing lived on my laptop.

Switched to SQLite and suddenly I didn't need a database container, environment variables for local credentials, or a setup script just to run the project.

Obviously I'm not suggesting SQLite for every production workload. But for prototypes, local tools and small apps, having a database that is literally one file is ridiculously convenient.

Sometimes the boring option is the good option.

title: I stopped using console.log as my entire debugging strategy
body:
Not completely. I still use it when I'm being lazy.

But once an app has enough moving parts, random console logs become surprisingly hard to follow. Especially when several requests are happening at the same time.

Adding request IDs to logs changed things for me. Now I can search for one request and actually follow it from the controller to the database call.

```txt
request=8f31 route=/orders/42
request=8f31 db.query started
request=8f31 db.query finished
request=8f31 response=200
```

It took maybe an hour to set up and has saved me much more than an hour of staring at terminal output.

title: CSS container queries finally clicked for me
body:
I kept thinking of responsive design as something controlled by the viewport. Then I tried container queries properly and it finally made sense.

A card doesn't really care whether the screen is 1440px wide. It cares how much space its parent gives it.

That sounds obvious now, but it changed how I think about reusable components. A component can decide how it looks based on its actual container instead of making assumptions about the whole page.

Still not using them everywhere, but for reusable cards and dashboard widgets they make a lot of sense.

title: What actually belongs in a Docker image?
body:
I spent too long building Docker images that contained basically the entire project, including files nobody needed at runtime.

A proper `.dockerignore` helped more than I expected. Then I switched to a multi-stage build so the final image only contained the production dependencies and compiled app.

The final image went from over 900MB to just under 200MB.

The funny thing is that the application itself barely changed. Most of the reduction came from simply being more deliberate about what was being copied into the image.

title: Don't make your frontend wait for everything
body:
I had a dashboard that showed a loading spinner until every API request finished. Five requests were happening in parallel, but the UI behaved like it was waiting for one giant request.

Changed it so each section renders as its own data arrives. The page feels dramatically faster even though the backend response times are exactly the same.

It's a small UX thing, but users don't experience your API timings directly. They experience how long they have to stare at a blank screen.

Sometimes perceived performance is just about not blocking useful UI on unrelated data.

title: My Express error handler was hiding the actual error
body:
We had an Express error handler that was doing this:

```js
res.status(500).json({ error: "Something went wrong" });
```

Very friendly for users. Completely useless for debugging.

The server logs weren't capturing the original error consistently either, so we ended up with a production issue where all we knew was that something had gone wrong. Incredible detective work.

I changed the middleware to log the original error with the request context, while keeping the response generic for clients.

The lesson isn't 'send stack traces to users'. Please don't. It's 'don't throw away useful information before you log it.'

title: A tiny accessibility fix that took five minutes
body:
Found a button in our app that was actually a `div` with a click handler.

It looked exactly like a button. Mouse users could click it. So nobody noticed.

Keyboard users couldn't focus it, screen readers didn't announce it properly, and pressing Enter didn't behave like a button.

Replaced it with an actual `<button>` and most of the accessibility problem disappeared immediately.

This is one of those cases where the accessible solution is also the simpler solution. No ARIA gymnastics required.

title: Why I started validating environment variables at startup
body:
Nothing ruins your morning like discovering that production has been running with a missing environment variable for three hours.

Our app used to discover configuration problems only when the relevant code path was hit. So the server could boot successfully and then randomly fail later.

Now we validate required config when the process starts. If something is missing, the app refuses to boot and tells us exactly what.

I'd rather have a container crash immediately than have a healthy-looking service quietly waiting to explode.

title: The SQL query was fine. The N+1 requests weren't.
body:
Spent an embarrassing amount of time optimizing a database query that wasn't actually the problem.

The page loaded 50 projects and then made another API request for each project's owner.

The database query itself was fast. We were just doing it 51 times.

Changed the endpoint to return the owner information with the projects and the load time dropped from around 2 seconds to a few hundred milliseconds.

N+1 is one of those problems that's so simple in hindsight. Unfortunately hindsight doesn't show up until after you've spent an afternoon staring at the wrong query.

title: Vite dev server spoiled me
body:
Went back to an older frontend project today and remembered what development used to feel like before Vite.

Started the app, changed one CSS rule, waited, stared at the screen, questioned my life choices.

Modern tooling has made the feedback loop so fast that going back to a slower setup feels painful now.

Obviously build tooling isn't the most important part of a project, but the development feedback loop matters more than I used to think. If it takes 20 seconds to see whether a tiny change worked, you're going to experiment less.

title: Git branches aren't a substitute for communication
body:
We had three people working on related parts of the same feature. Everyone had their own branch, everything was committed, and somehow we still managed to surprise each other with changes.

The problem wasn't Git. Nobody had clearly said what they were changing.

One person changed the API response while another was building the frontend against the old shape. Both were technically working correctly.

A five-minute conversation before starting would have saved us an hour of merge conflict archaeology.

title: Prisma migrations saved me from my own database habits
body:
I used to make small database changes manually during development and then try to remember what I had changed later.

That worked until another developer pulled the project and got a completely different schema.

Started using Prisma migrations properly and the workflow is much less chaotic. The schema changes are committed, the migration history is part of the project, and setting up a fresh database is predictable.

The database stopped being this mysterious thing that existed somewhere on my laptop.

title: I finally learned what CORS is actually doing
body:
For the longest time my mental model of CORS was basically 'the browser randomly hates my API'.

Turns out the browser is checking whether a different origin is allowed to make a request, and some requests trigger a preflight before the real request is sent.

Once I understood that, the network tab suddenly made much more sense. Seeing an OPTIONS request before my POST stopped looking like some mysterious extra request.

Still think the error messages could be friendlier, though. 'Blocked by CORS policy' is technically useful and emotionally useless.

title: When a simple boolean isn't actually simple
body:
Had a settings field called `notificationsEnabled` that looked harmless enough.

Then product added email notifications, push notifications and weekly summaries.

Suddenly one boolean wasn't enough because 'notifications' wasn't one thing anymore.

We changed the model to represent each preference separately. More fields, but much less ambiguity.

A lot of technical debt starts with perfectly reasonable assumptions that stop being true six months later. The trick is noticing when the model has outgrown the assumption.

title: Lazy loading images made a bigger difference than expected
body:
Our landing page had a bunch of images below the fold that were all loading immediately.

Nothing looked obviously broken, but the initial page load was heavier than it needed to be.

Added lazy loading to images that weren't visible initially and compressed a few of the larger assets. The page felt noticeably quicker on mobile connections.

It's easy to obsess over JavaScript bundle size while ignoring the giant 2MB JPEG sitting halfway down the page.

title: Testing the boring stuff caught the interesting bug
body:
I wrote what I thought was a pointless test for a date formatter because the function was only about ten lines long.

Then the test failed because dates near midnight were being formatted using the server's timezone instead of the user's timezone.

That bug would have been really annoying to reproduce manually.

This is why I keep changing my mind about 'obvious' code. If something depends on dates, timezones, rounding or user input, it probably deserves a test even when the implementation looks trivial.

title: The best refactor I made this week removed code
body:
I had a utility function that was being used in three places. I thought it was a perfect candidate for making it more generic.

So I added options. Then more options. Then a callback. Eventually I realized the three places didn't actually have enough in common to justify the abstraction.

Deleted the utility and put the small pieces back where they belonged.

The codebase got shorter and easier to understand.

I think I sometimes confuse 'less duplicated code' with 'better code'. Duplication can be cheaper than a complicated abstraction.
